question.leadin: This man fought Huascar (WAHS-car) during the War of the Two Brothers.
question.text: Name this ruler who was strangled at the hands of Spanish conquistadors after converting to Christianity. He lost his capital of Cuzco to the Spanish when he failed to fill a room with gold.
question.clue: He offered to fill a large room with gold and silver for his ransom, but the Spaniards didn't release him.

swap.text: This Spaniard led the war against the Incas and ordered the execution of Atahualpa, even though Atahualpa offered to give this man a room filled with gold.
swap.clue: This man received help from longtime partner Diego Almagro, but he was killed by Almagro's forces in the Battle of Las Salinas.

question.text: This Incan "lost city" is believed to have been built for Pachacuti. It was re-discovered in 1911 by Hiram Bingham.
question.clue: It is believed that it served as a retreat for Pachacuti Yupanqui, who had conquered the region of Tampu.

swap.text: Diego de Ordaz is one conquistador who looked for the ceremonial place where this mythical chief covered himself in gold and jumped into a lake. The term is Spanish for "the golden one."
swap.clue: During the first part of the journey in which Orellana travelled the length of the Amazon, a valley of Cinnamon and this place were the targets of Gonzalo Pizzaro.

question.leadin: This country fought the Cenepa and Paquisha Wars against its northern neighbor, Ecuador.
question.text: Name this country, home to the cities of Arequipa and its capital, Lima.
question.clue: That culture in this country was also responsible for creating a series of images called Lines near Palpa that are well-known geoglyphs.

swap.text: The Incas used these sets of knotted, threaded strings to count gold, corn, and other goods. They were also used for record-keeping.
swap.clue: Evidence for a writing system in these objects include a three-number sequence possibly representing the village of Puruchuco (poo-roo-CHOO-koh).

question.text: After sacking Ankara in Turkey, Tamerlane allegedly made a pyramid of these objects.
question.clue: Timur allegedly built pyramids out of these body parts, the protective structure for the brain, which would terrify his enemies.

swap.leadin: Titus Salt made Bradford, England a center of processing fiber imported from this country's alpacas.
swap.text: Name this coastal Andean country that, with Bolivia, fought the War of the Pacific against its southern neighbor, Chile.
swap.clue: This country's native leader Tupac Amaru rebelled in 1780 and Jose de San Martin became its Protector in 1821.

question.leadin: The artist Cecilia Vicuna often hangs artworks named for these objects from ceilings.
question.text: Name these objects that were used for record-keeping and other purposes by the Inca.
question.clue: This devices that were made of string and were commonly used for keeping census records or for monitoring taxes. The information on these devices was stored using knots.

swap.leadin: Pachacuti transformed the Kingdom of Cuzco into this empire.
swap.text: Name this civilization of modern-day Peru which was conquered by Francisco Pizarro.
swap.clue: After the Battle of Cajamarca , Atahualpa was captured and executed by Francisco Pizarro, ending this polity.

question.leadin: Answer the following about remote sensing and the usage of aerial technology in archaeology.
question.text: While flying, Paul Kosok realized that what he believed were irrigation canals in a desert were actually animal-shaped lines, named for this civilization of southern Peru.
question.clue: Paul Kosok and Maria Reiche (RAI-keh) mapped structures created by these people.

swap.leadin: Early colonial writer Juan Freyle wrote an account of a ceremony in which a new ruler of these people was covered in gold dust and submerged in Lake Guatavita.
swap.text: Name this confederation of Northern Andean tribes that was led by co-rulers called Zipa and Zaque. They were encountered by the Conquistador Gonzalo Jimenez de Quesada after his expedition sailed up the Magdalena.
swap.clue: This people, whose confederation was ruled by a zipa in the south and a zaque in the north. The last powerful cacique of these people, Tundama, was killed with a large hammer by Balthasar Maldonado.

question.text: This emperor of the Inca wrote special hymns for the Situa Festival. This man, whose name means "Earthshaker," pacified the Chanca peoples and his son, Tupo Inca, built the Saqsaywaman Fort in Cusco.
question.clue: This ruler, who legendarily subjugated the (+) Chanka people with stone warriors, organized his realm into four suyus.

swap.leadin: These structures were first described as trail markers in the 1553 Cronicas del Peru by Pedro Cieza de Leon.
swap.text: Name these geoglyphs found in their namesake desert in southern Peru that include a hummingbird and spider. Some people think that aliens made these geoglyphs, as they can only be seen in full from above.
swap.clue: These things were damaged by Greenpeace activists wearing improper footwear as part of a 2014 protest.

question.text: The Acari Valley had previously been ruled by these people, some of whose puquios aqueducts are still used today.
question.clue: This culture built the Cantalloc ("cahn-TAH-yoke")Aqueducts, exemplifying the corkscrew entrances of their puquios ("poo-KEE-ohʼs").

swap.leadin: Structures built by this civilization shared many commonalities with ritual centers built in the contemporary Kotosh religious tradition style.
swap.text: Name this ancient civilization in modern-day Peru, the oldest-known civilization in the Americas. The MFAC theory regarding the beginning of this civilization has been heavily undermined by further excavation.

question.leadin: By the Late Pleistocene, these weapons likely took down guanacos and rheas in Patagonia, where horse cultures wielding them arose by the 17th century.
question.text: Name these weapons that Querandi ("kair-ahn-DEE") game hunters may have introduced to the Diaguita ("dee-ah-GHEE-tah") Confederacy. Gauchos adopted these roped throwing stones to fell cattle.
question.answerHtml: bolas [or bolas de piedra or boleadoras or boleadeiras; accept bola perdida; prompt on balls or projectiles]

swap.leadin: A Spanish proverb says that to be "worth a" this city is to be worth a fortune.
swap.text: Name this city in Bolivia that was the location of the Spanish colonial mint and the major supplier of silver for Spain during their colonial empire days. The mines here were mythically founded by Huayna Capac.
swap.clue: Workers in this city still give offerings to a goat-headed underworld deity called "The Uncle" or El Tio.

question.leadin: They were put forth by the namesake Count of Oropesa and overturned the New Laws of Blasco Nunez Vela.
question.text: Name this set of structural changes put forth in the 1570s, which created "reductions" of native population governed by kuraka, and established the mita system for forced labor in the silver mines.
question.clue: Spain revived the mita system in this series of late 16th-century laws, which installed Inca regional leaders called kurakas as the head of repartimientos, or groups of natives from whom labor could be levied.

swap.text: Peruvian magnates on these islands hired blackbirders to kidnap workers to mine guano. Spain seized these islands to acquire those mines in the 1860s, but was repulsed by a coalition of South American countries.
swap.clue: Kidnapped Chinese workers were also kept in slave-like conditions on these Peruvian islands in order to harvest guano. Spain seized these islands in 1864, which prompted a war in which Chile and Peru fought to take them back.
